strings.travel_commentary_note: Two of these manuals print a base text and a commentary together. The Risala is Ibn Abi Zayd’s text with al-Azhari’s commentary in square brackets; Umdat al-Fiqh is Ibn Qudamah’s text with Hatem al-Haj’s notes. Where a ruling here rests on the commentary rather than the base text, the entry says so.
strings.travel_d_begin_p1: Once you have passed the last buildings of your area and the adjoining town-land — a cemetery or common ground that belongs to the town. You need not pass farms or orchards beyond that. From that point you may shorten even before you have covered the 81 km.
strings.travel_d_begin_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Shortening Of Prayer; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Conditions That Validate The Intention Of Travel
strings.travel_d_begin_p2: After passing the town wall, if there is one; otherwise after the last houses, not counting farmland, orchards and graveyards. Where one town’s buildings run into the next, the journey begins at the edge people recognise as the town’s limit. A desert-dweller starts once past his people’s tents.
strings.travel_d_begin_p3: Not until every house of the town is behind you, with none in front or level with you. The Risala’s commentary notes a minority view that from a Friday-prayer town you do not shorten until three miles past its edge; the school’s usual position is simply the end of the buildings.
strings.travel_d_begin_p4: Umdat al-Fiqh, in the part read, defines the journey by its distance and does not say where along the way the shortening may begin. The guide does not supply a Hanbali answer here.
strings.travel_d_begin_subject: The point at which shortening may start.
strings.travel_d_distance_p1: A journey of three days’ travel, measured at an ordinary pace — a loaded camel or a person on foot — over the short days of the year, with the nights for rest. Nur al-Idah adds that scholars have since reckoned this at about 81 kilometres one way, by any means of transport.
strings.travel_d_distance_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Travel Due To Which The Rules Change; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Conditions That Validate The Intention Of Travel
strings.travel_d_distance_p2: At least 48 mil (Hashimi miles) one way — which Reliance’s translator gives as roughly 81 km, or 50 miles. The same distance applies by land or by sea, and it is the distance that counts, not how long the trip takes.
strings.travel_d_distance_p2_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f15.1, f15.2
strings.travel_d_distance_p3: Four burud, which the Risala states as forty-eight miles. Its commentary puts this at about a day and a night’s travel by pack animals, and reports smaller disputed figures below that — a repeat is owed for shortening at 35 miles, not at 40; Ibn Rushd is cited for 36.
strings.travel_d_distance_p4: The text of Umdat al-Fiqh gives sixteen farsakhs — about a two-day journey at a moderate pace, which its note works out to roughly 89 km or 50 miles. But the same note records that Ibn Qudamah in his larger work al-Mughni, with others, sets no fixed minimum at all: any trip that people would call travelling.
strings.travel_d_distance_p4_src: Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 11: Prayer of the Traveler
strings.travel_d_distance_subject: The shortest journey that permits shortening.
strings.travel_d_imam_p1: If the prayer is being prayed in its own time, the traveller follows and completes all four raka’at with the imam — the shortening is set aside. If its time has already gone, a traveller may not follow a resident imam for it at all, though a traveller may lead residents in either case.
strings.travel_d_imam_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — A Traveller Praying Behind A Resident And Vice Versa
strings.travel_d_imam_p2: A traveller loses the dispensation the moment he prays any part of the prayer behind an imam who is not shortening. He then owes the full four, and an intention to shorten formed behind such an imam does not hold.
strings.travel_d_imam_p2_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f15.8, f12.28
strings.travel_d_imam_p3: A traveller who joins the resident imam for a whole raka’ah or more prays the full four; joining later than that — under a raka’ah — he prays two. This is from the Risala’s commentary, citing ad-Dakhira, not from Ibn Abi Zayd’s text.
strings.travel_d_imam_p4: The traveller completes the prayer behind a resident imam — all four — even if he joined only moments before the closing salam. This is stated in Hatem al-Haj’s notes on Umdat al-Fiqh.
strings.travel_d_imam_p4_src: Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 11: Prayer of the Traveler
strings.travel_d_imam_subject: What a traveller does behind a resident imam.
strings.travel_d_join_rain_p1: Not done, on the same chapter that rules out joining for travel: the exception it names is the hajj joining, and nothing else.
strings.travel_d_join_rain_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Not Joining Two Obligatory Prayers In the One Time
strings.travel_d_join_rain_p2: Permitted, but only forward — Dhuhr with Asr in Dhuhr’s time, or Maghrib with Isha in Maghrib’s time, never the reverse. It must be rain heavy enough to wet the clothes, you must be praying in a group in a mosque that is a real distance away, and it must be raining as the first prayer begins and ends and as the second begins.
strings.travel_d_join_rain_p2_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f15.14, f15.15, f15.17
strings.travel_d_join_rain_p3: Permitted for Maghrib and Isha only — not Dhuhr and Asr. The Risala allows it for a lot of rain, and also for thick mud together with a moonless dark, but not for mud alone or dark alone. Melted snow and cold count as rain.
strings.travel_d_join_rain_p4: Permitted for Maghrib and Isha in rain. Umdat al-Fiqh’s note adds that on Ahmad’s view a severe wind and cold, and muddy streets even without rain, fall under the same rule.
strings.travel_d_join_rain_p4_src: Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 10: The Prayer of The Sick — Where Else Is Combining Prayers Permissible?
strings.travel_d_join_sick_p1: Not done. The chapter that forbids joining for travel or rain leaves no room for an illness case either.
strings.travel_d_join_sick_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Not Joining Two Obligatory Prayers In the One Time
strings.travel_d_join_sick_p2: Not a ground in the Shafi’i school. Reliance states that the school has no reason for joining other than travel and rain — and notes that the Hanbali school does allow it for a sick person, a nursing mother and others.
strings.travel_d_join_sick_p3: Permitted. The Risala allows a sick person to join when they fear losing consciousness before the next prayer’s time, and again when an illness such as a bad stomach makes getting up for each prayer a real hardship.
strings.travel_d_join_sick_p4: Permitted when praying each prayer in its own time is hard for the sick person. Umdat al-Fiqh grounds this on the Prophet ﷺ allowing a woman with prolonged bleeding to join her prayers, and asks for the same intention and continuity as the traveller’s joining.
strings.travel_d_join_sick_p4_src: Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 10: The Prayer of The Sick — Combining Prayers for the Sick
strings.travel_d_join_travel_p1: Not done. Nur al-Idah gives this its own short chapter and rules it out: two obligatory prayers may not be prayed in one time slot, not for a journey and not for rain. The only joining it allows anywhere is on hajj — Dhuhr with Asr at Arafah, and Maghrib with Isha at Muzdalifa, prayed with the imam and in ihram.
strings.travel_d_join_travel_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Not Joining Two Obligatory Prayers In the One Time; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Prayer Of The Traveller
strings.travel_d_join_travel_p2: Permitted on a journey that qualifies for shortening. The pair may be prayed together in either prayer’s slot — the earlier one’s or the later one’s. Joining in the earlier slot needs the intention before you finish that prayer and no long gap after it. As with shortening, Reliance holds it better not to take the dispensation.
strings.travel_d_join_travel_p2_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f15.9, f15.10, f15.12
strings.travel_d_join_travel_p3: Permitted for hard travelling, but as a formal joining: the earlier prayer is held back to the close of its own window and the later one pulled forward to the open of its, so neither actually leaves its slot. The Risala’s commentary allows a fuller joining — the second prayer moved back into the first’s time — for someone with a real excuse such as a journey.
strings.travel_d_join_travel_p4: Permitted for any traveller who may shorten, in the time of either prayer. Umdat al-Fiqh asks that you intend the join before the first prayer and keep the two together, separated by no more than the time to make wudu; it notes that Ibn Taymiya did not treat the intention as a condition.
strings.travel_d_join_travel_p4_src: Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 10: The Prayer of The Sick — Where Else Is Combining Prayers Permissible?; Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 10: The Prayer of The Sick — Combining Prayers for the Sick
strings.travel_d_join_travel_subject: Joining Dhuhr with Asr, or Maghrib with Isha, on a journey.
strings.travel_d_ruling_p1: Binding (wajib). Nur al-Idah argues that the traveller’s prayer was revealed as two raka’at in the first place, so shortening is not a concession (rukhsa) but the prayer in its original form — an ‘azimah. On that basis the school holds a traveller must shorten.
strings.travel_d_ruling_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Ruling Of Shortening
strings.travel_d_ruling_p2: A dispensation you may take or leave. Reliance’s translator adds a note at f15.0 that in the Shafi’i school it is better not to take a dispensation that is merely permitted — so praying the full four is a good choice, not a failing. That is his note, not Ibn Naqib’s text.
strings.travel_d_ruling_p2_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f15.0 (translator’s note); Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Ruling Of Shortening
strings.travel_d_ruling_p3: A confirmed sunna — firmer than a bare permission, but short of an obligation. This grading is from al-Azhari’s commentary; Ibn Abi Zayd’s base text simply says you should shorten. Nur al-Idah, reporting the schools, likewise puts Malik’s view at “sunna, not wajib”.
strings.travel_d_ruling_p3_src: The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 14.1a; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Ruling Of Shortening
strings.travel_d_ruling_p4: A dispensation. Umdat al-Fiqh states plainly that the traveller may pray the full number, and that shortening is the better of the two.
strings.travel_d_ruling_p4_src: Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 11: Prayer of the Traveler
strings.travel_d_ruling_subject: The standing of shortening on a journey.
strings.travel_d_stay_p1: Fifteen days. Intend to stay somewhere fifteen days or more and you pray in full from arrival. Intend less than that, or fix no length, and you keep shortening for as long as you are there. Nur al-Idah cites Ibn Umar shortening for six months snowed in at Azerbaijan.
strings.travel_d_stay_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Period Of Shortening Prayers; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — When Is An Intention Of Residing Not Valid
strings.travel_d_stay_p2: Four full days — the day you arrive and the day you leave not counted. Beyond that you pray in full. The one stretch: if you are held up by a task you expect to finish and be gone at any moment, you may keep shortening up to 18 days, then pray in full.
strings.travel_d_stay_p3: Four days, or twenty prayers — the day you arrive not counted. Intend that much and you pray in full until you move on. An army halted in hostile territory is the exception and keeps shortening.
strings.travel_d_stay_p4: More than twenty-one prayers — four days and one prayer. Intend to stay longer than that and you complete your prayers; with no such intention you shorten indefinitely. Umdat al-Fiqh reports agreement on the open-ended case and notes that only the Shafi’i school caps it, at 18 days.
strings.travel_d_stay_p4_src: Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 11: Prayer of the Traveler
strings.travel_d_stay_subject: The intended length of stay that ends shortening.
strings.travel_editions: Each school’s position is cited to a manual of that school: Reliance of the Traveller for Shafi’i, Nur al-Idah for Hanafi, The Risala for Maliki, Umdat al-Fiqh for Hanbali. Section numbers follow the English editions listed here.
strings.travel_hadith_edition: Hadith numbering follows the numbering used on Sunnah.com, which generally aligns with widely published editions.
strings.travel_intro: On a journey the five daily prayers still have to be prayed — but two things change. The four-raka’ah prayers may be prayed as two, and two prayers may be moved into a single time slot so you are not stopping twice. The first is called shortening (qasr); the second is joining (jam’). They are separate: you can do one without the other. This guide covers what counts as a journey, when the dispensations start and stop, which prayers they touch, and where the four schools differ — including the one every traveller should know, that shortening is not simply optional in every school. Joining is also allowed for rain, and in some schools for illness, so those are here too.
strings.travel_s10_agree_1: On a lawful journey of roughly a day’s travel or more, the four-raka’ah prayers — Dhuhr, Asr and Isha — are prayed as two raka’at.
strings.travel_s10_agree_2: Fajr and Maghrib are never shortened, at home or travelling.
strings.travel_s10_agree_3: Shortening begins only after leaving the town, and ends on reaching home.
strings.travel_s10_agree_4: A pilgrim joins Dhuhr with Asr at Arafah, and Maghrib with Isha at Muzdalifa.
strings.travel_s10_agree_5: A traveller who prays behind a resident imam in that prayer’s time prays the full four with him.
strings.travel_s10_agree_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f15.1, f15.6, f15.7, f15.8; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Shortening Of Prayer; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Not Joining Two Obligatory Prayers In the One Time; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — A Traveller Praying Behind A Resident And Vice Versa; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 14.1b, 14.1d, 12.6f; Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 11: Prayer of the Traveler
strings.travel_s10_body: Under the differences above, all four schools hold that:
strings.travel_s10_differ: They differ on the points this guide marks: the minimum distance and how it is measured, whether shortening is required or optional, how long a stay makes you resident again, whether and how you may join prayers on a journey, whether you may join for rain or for illness, and what a traveller does behind a resident imam.
strings.travel_s1_body: Not every trip is a journey in the eyes of the law. The dispensations begin only once you intend to travel at least a set minimum distance, for a lawful purpose. A short trip across town, or an outing with no destination, changes nothing — you pray as you do at home.
strings.travel_s1_distance_intro: The minimum distance is the first thing the schools disagree on, and they measure it in different units — days of travel, miles, and older road-stages. The figures below are each manual’s own, with the modern estimate it gives. Do not treat them as one number.
strings.travel_s1_purpose: The purpose of the trip matters too. In the Shafi’i, Maliki and Hanbali schools a journey taken in order to disobey Allah — the manuals instance travelling to commit a theft, or a woman travelling where her husband has forbidden — carries no dispensation; you pray in full. The Hanafi school does not draw this line: a Hanafi traveller shortens even on a sinful journey, though the sin itself is a separate matter.
strings.travel_s1_purpose_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f15.5; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Shortening Of Prayer; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 14.1c
strings.travel_s1_route: If there are two roads to where you are going and you take the longer one for a real reason — safety, an easier road, seeing something on the way — you may still shorten, provided the trip itself has a genuine purpose. Taking the long way round only to unlock the dispensation does not count.
strings.travel_s2_body: Intending to travel is not enough on its own. Shortening starts once you have actually left the built-up part of your town behind you, and it stops when you are home again — or earlier, if you settle somewhere for long enough, which the next section covers.
strings.travel_s2_end: Shortening ends the moment your journey does. All four schools agree it ends when you reach your home town; the Maliki school adds that it ends once you come within about a mile of it. It also ends — before you get home — when you form a firm intention to stay put somewhere, and the length that takes is the next section.
strings.travel_s2_end_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f15.7; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Period Of Shortening Prayers; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 14.1e; Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 11: Prayer of the Traveler
strings.travel_s2_heading: When shortening begins, and when it ends
strings.travel_s3_body: This is the number a traveller actually needs. If you break your journey and stay in one place, at some point you count as resident again and must pray in full. The schools set that point differently, and the difference is large. One rule they share: if you never form an intention to stay — you keep expecting to leave the next day, and simply do not — you may go on shortening indefinitely. The Companions are reported to have shortened for months, even years, in that state.
strings.travel_s3_heading: How long you may keep shortening if you stop somewhere
strings.travel_s4_body: Only the three four-raka’ah prayers are shortened, and only to two raka’at: Dhuhr, Asr and Isha. Fajr stays two raka’at and Maghrib stays three, on a journey exactly as at home. All four schools agree on this, and the Maliki and Hanbali manuals report it as a point of consensus.
strings.travel_s4_body_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f15.1; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Shortening Of Prayer; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 14.1b, 8.4a; Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 11: Prayer of the Traveler
strings.travel_s4_hadith: A’isha said the prayer was first made obligatory as two raka’at, and that the traveller’s prayer stayed as it was while the resident’s was raised to four. Maghrib and the dawn prayer were the two not raised — and they are the two a traveller does not shorten either.
strings.travel_s4_hadith_src: Sahih al-Bukhari 1090; Sahih Muslim 685; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 14.1b; Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 11: Prayer of the Traveler
strings.travel_s4_heading: Which prayers shorten, and which never do
strings.travel_s4_makeup: A prayer missed on the journey and made up later is a special case. The Hanafi and Maliki manuals fix its length by your state when its time ran out: missed while travelling, it is made up as two even after you are home; missed while resident, made up as four even while you travel. The Missed Prayers guide covers make-ups in full.
strings.travel_s4_makeup_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Making Up Missed Prayers; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 14.1a
strings.travel_s5_body: Most people meet shortening as a permission — a nice-to-have you can take or leave. That is true in two schools and not in the other two, and the difference is not academic: a Hanafi traveller who prays four raka’at has left something the school considers binding, while a Shafi’i or Hanbali one has only declined a dispensation.
strings.travel_s5_hadith: When Umar was asked why Muslims still shorten though the fear the Qur’an mentions has passed, he said he had asked the Prophet ﷺ the same, and was told, “It is an act of charity Allah has given you, so accept His charity.”
strings.travel_s5_hanafi_note: For a Hanafi traveller this has a concrete edge. If he prays four and does sit for the middle tashahhud, the prayer counts but is disliked, and the last two raka’at are reckoned voluntary. If he prays four without that middle sitting, the obligatory prayer is invalid — unless he had decided to stay and become resident as he stood for the third.
strings.travel_s5_hanafi_note_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Ruling Of Shortening
strings.travel_s5_heading: Is shortening required, or only allowed?
strings.travel_s6_arafah: One joining is uncontested: on hajj, the pilgrims pray Dhuhr and Asr together at Arafah in the early afternoon, and Maghrib and Isha together on reaching Muzdalifa. Even Nur al-Idah, which allows no other joining, sets this apart as its own case — prayed with the imam, and in ihram. The Risala ranks it a strong sunna.
strings.travel_s6_arafah_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Not Joining Two Obligatory Prayers In the One Time; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 12.6f, 12.6g
strings.travel_s6_body: Joining (jam’) means praying Dhuhr and Asr together, or Maghrib and Isha together, in one of their two time slots — so a traveller who cannot easily stop twice stops once. It is a different dispensation from shortening: three schools let a traveller do both, one at either time; one school does not allow joining on a journey at all.
strings.travel_s6_heading: Joining two prayers on a journey
strings.travel_s6_shortening_link: Joining does not shorten anything. If you join Dhuhr and Asr on a journey you still pray each of them as two raka’at, for the reason in the section above; joined Maghrib is still three.
strings.travel_s6_shortening_link_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f15.1, f15.9
strings.travel_s7_body: Joining is not only a traveller’s dispensation. Heavy rain is a separate ground for it in three schools, and illness in two — so a resident whose school allows it need not guess. The Hanafi school, which does not join for travel, does not join for these either.
strings.travel_s7_heading: Joining for rain, and for illness
strings.travel_s8_body: Two situations that come up in any mosque away from home: a traveller who prays behind a resident imam, and a resident who prays behind a travelling imam. The first is where the schools part; the second they broadly agree on.
strings.travel_s8_hadith: Nur al-Idah anchors this in a hadith: the Prophet ﷺ, leading the people of Mecca while he was himself travelling, told them, “Make your prayer complete; we are a company of travellers.”
strings.travel_s8_hadith_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — A Traveller Praying Behind A Resident And Vice Versa; the wording is also carried in Malik’s Muwatta
strings.travel_s8_heading: A traveller and a resident praying together
strings.travel_s8_reverse: The reverse — a resident praying behind a travelling imam — is spelled out plainly only by Nur al-Idah: the imam prays his two raka’at and gives salam (it is recommended he tell the congregation beforehand that he is travelling), and the residents then stand and finish the remaining two on their own, without reciting. The other three manuals, in the parts read for this guide, do not treat this case separately.
strings.travel_s8_reverse_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — A Traveller Praying Behind A Resident And Vice Versa
strings.travel_s9_body: The dispensations are about the obligatory prayers. The voluntary prayers are touched much less, and the manuals read for this guide say less about them — but a few points are clear.
strings.travel_s9_gap: The Risala and Umdat al-Fiqh, in the chapters read for this guide, do not set out a traveller’s rule for the regular sunna prayers, and the guide does not fill that in.
strings.travel_s9_hanafi: For a Hanafi traveller, Witr keeps its standing as a necessary (wajib) prayer and is prayed as at home. Nur al-Idah, in the part read, does not lay out which of the other regular sunna prayers a traveller keeps or leaves.
strings.travel_s9_hanafi_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Chapter Of Witr
strings.travel_s9_riding: One point that is not disputed: a voluntary prayer — never an obligatory one — may be prayed while riding, facing whatever way the mount is going. Nur al-Idah gives this its own chapter.
strings.travel_s9_riding_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Voluntary Prayer Upon A Beast (Or Means Of Transport)
strings.travel_s9_shafii: Reliance defines the ten confirmed sunna raka’at — before Fajr, before and after Dhuhr, after Maghrib, after Isha — precisely as the ones the Prophet ﷺ kept up “whether travelling or at home”. In the Shafi’i school, then, a traveller still prays them.
strings.travel_src_nur: Nur al-Idah, Hasan al-Shurunbulali — Hanafi. Book ii (Prayer): the chapters from “Prayer Of The Traveller” onward, and “Not Joining Two Obligatory Prayers In the One Time”, were read directly for this guide.
strings.travel_src_reliance: Reliance of the Traveller (Umdat al-Salik), Ahmad ibn Naqib al-Misri, tr. Nuh Ha Mim Keller — Shafi’i. Section f15 (“Shortening or Joining Prayers for Travel or Rain”), with f10.2 and f12.28, was read directly for this guide.
strings.travel_src_risala: The Risala, Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani, tr. Bello Mohammad Daura, with the commentary of al-Azhari — Maliki. Chapter 12.6 (“Joining prayers”), chapter 14 (“On Travelling Prayers”), and 8.4a and 23.12 were read directly for this guide.
strings.travel_src_umdah: Umdat al-Fiqh, Ibn Qudamah al-Maqdisi, translated with commentary by Hatem al-Haj — Hanbali. Book 2, chapter 11 (“Prayer of the Traveler”) and chapter 10 (“The Prayer of The Sick”, on combining) were read directly. This edition is an abridgement: where it does not cover a question, the guide says so.
strings.travel_summary: Shortening on a journey, and joining two prayers into one time
strings.travel_unreviewed: No qualified scholar has checked this guide. Every ruling in it was checked against a manual of the school it is credited to, and names where — but that verifies the transcription, not the fiqh. Treat this as a draft and ask someone qualified before you rely on it.
